review_comments.author: Richard Cheng
review_comments.summary: Reviewer Richard Cheng questioned the design of private memory NUMA nodes, specifically how they interact with existing abstractions like CXL protocols and zonelists. He noted that CXL protocols only define physical/transport-level rules for memory transactions, leaving it to the OS to decide how to manage devices. He also pointed out that the current implementation does not consider supporting a global zonelist with multiple private nodes, instead opting for separate dedicated zonelists. Cheng expressed concerns about implicit opt-ins and unclear behavior in reclaim paths when iterating over all zones on all private nodes.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Wed, Jul 22, 2026 at 11:40:06AM +0800, Gregory Price wrote:
> On Wed, Jul 22, 2026 at 10:20:00PM +0800, Richard Cheng wrote:
> > On Mon, Jul 20, 2026 at 03:33:54PM +0800, Gregory Price wrote:
> > Hi Gregory,
> > 
> > I applied your series on mm-next and give a quick review,
> > not thoroughly, still I have some questions below regarding the design.
> >  
> 
> Hi Richard,
> 
> Thank you for the read.
> 
> Just a heads up, this was based on mm-new because of some recent work
> on Brendan's page_alloc.h cleanup, but if you managed to get it applied
> then maybe that's made its way forward already.
> 
> > > The goal here is to flip that dynamic, isolate by default and then
> > > opt-in to specific services that the device says is safe.
> > > 
> > > Isolation at the NUMA/Zonelist layer provides a powerful mechanism for
> > > memory hosted on accelerators - re-use of the kernel mm/ code.
> > > 
> > >  - Accelerators (GPUs) can use demotion, numactl, and reclaim.
> > >  - Special memory devices (Compressed RAM) with special access controls
> > >    (promote-on-write) can have generic services written for them.
> > >  - Network devices with large memory regions intended for ring buffers
> > >    can use the buddy and standard networking stack.
> > >  - Slow, disaggregated memory pools which aren't suitable as general
> > >    purpose memory get cleaner interfaces (no need to re-write the buddy
> > >    in userland, can use migration interface, etc).
> > >  - Per-workload dedicated memory nodes (disaggregated VM memory)
> > > 
> > 
> > For accelerator part, take CXL Type-2 as example, it has its own protocol
> > CXL.cache, CXL.mem which is the rule they need to obey during memory transaction,
> > Adding more rules for them since they are NUMA node confused me, I wonder the reason ?
> > 
> 
> CXL protocols simply state how to do the memory transaction at a
> physical / transport level.  It does not make any statement on how the
> operating systems are to make sense of these devices or what constructs
> / abstractions to build to actually manage the devices themselves.
>

Ahhh thanks this clears my question.
Then this abstraction makes sense.

> This series is not necessarily attached to CXL in particular, you could
> just as easily carve out memory from the general pool onto a private
> node to ensure it only gets used for a particular use.
> 
> In fact, that is how I have been testing this with dax/kmem:
> https://github.com/gourryinverse/linux/commit/f279e741d9c3643597525bfab916b29b95cb635b
> 
> > Because NUMA node, at least for me, representing topology/locality rather than
> > something with ownership or capability or rules.
> > 
> 
> The NUMA abstraction representing topology/locality is a construct we
> (the OS developers) have decided on historically - but there's nothing
> that dictates we can never create new useful abstractions with it.
> 
> Consider:
>     N_NORMAL_MEMORY,        /* The node has regular memory */
>     N_HIGH_MEMORY,          /* The node has regular or high memory */
> 
> These have nothing to do with topology or locality, they are node states
> that only have meaning in the context of linux mm/.
> 

Ok, I see.

> 
> To make something clear - there is no *requirement* for any particular
> device to use this abstraction.  It simply enables a cleaner way for
> devices carrying memory to re-utilize mm/ services while ensuring their
> memory does not silently get used under system pressure (or some vagrant
> in userspace doing `numactl --interleave all`).
> 
> Ignoring all the CAP bits entirely, if you just took the base series
> your driver could re-use the buddy allocator without any special logic
> AND have confidence that your driver is the only possible user of that
> memory (barring some truly obscene bug).
> 
> > >  - isolation via a dedicated zonelist:
> > >      - private nodes are omitted from FALLBACK/NOFALLBACK
> > >      - added ZONELIST_PRIVATE(_NOFALLBACK)
> > 
> > I saw the reply in patch 5, so in fact there's not only one
> > dedicate zonelist, but numerous ?
> > I raise the question because zonelist was supposed to be a
> > global, unbypasssable thing in MM design, but now what you
> > are trying to do is to seperate the whole global list into several
> > parts ?
> > 
> > Can you explain why in current design you don't consider to support
> > something like ZONELIST_PRIVATE[n]={0, .. ,n-1} ? that's my imagination
> > of what a global zonelist should look like, no matter private or non.
> > 
> 
> First let me say that there's nothing that prevents us from doing this,
> and we *could* make this the default case - but this decision was
> intentional by me.
> 
> Having them all present in each-other's zonelists by default creates a
> number of implicit opt-ins that are unclear:
> 
>   - any direct zonelist iterator now iterates all zones on all private
>     nodes, even those nodes do not opt into the same services
> 
>     e.g. zonelist iteration in reclaim that targets Private Node A would
>     attempt to reclaim Private Node B as well.  That would require and
>     extra explicit filter.
> 
>     I ask: Why do this? Just isolate in the zonelist, and if there is
>            a desire for intersections - make it explicit, not implicit.
> 

Fair enough, thanks for the headup.

>   - fallback allocations can now occur across private nodes, even
>     if those nodes are intended for different purposes.
> 
>     Obviously you can use nodemask to tighten the allocation target, but
>     I use `numactl --interleave --all` as an example of a clear case
>     where intersected nodelists may not give you the behavior you want.
> 
> 
> So for consistency - everything including zonelists have full isolation.
> This way all interactions with a private node must be explicit - always.
> 

Good choice I think, avoiding those implicit opt-in assumption will make
future developers more aware of things and do not just stumble into them.

> 
> This is actually one of the problems with ZONE_DEVICE - and you can see
> it in this patch set.  Some of the hooks in mm/ for zone_device only
> apply to PTE cases, and are absent from PMD cases - only because PMD
> mappings in ZONE_DEVICE aren't supported.
> 
> That kind of implicit behavior is quite bad.
> 
> That said, future improvements could include something like:
> 
> for_reclaimable_zone(ZONELIST_PRIVATE) {}
> 
> where we loosen this isolation, and formalize a filter, but I would
> like to see the usecase for it first.  Loosening the isolation defeats
> the entire purpose of the series, so there should be a strong reason to
> do so.

Totally agree.

> 
> > > Allocation Isolation
> > > ====================
> > > page_alloc presently controls whether a node's memory can be allocated
> > > on a given call by 4 things (in order of authority)
> > > 
> > >   1) ZONELIST membership
> > >      If a node is not in the walked zonelist, it's unreachable.
> > >
> > 
> > So a device gets hotplugged in the system will get a dedicated zonelist here ?
> 
> Yes.
> 
> > And make sure it obeys the device's own protocol if it has one ?
> > 
> 
> I'm not sure i follow this question, can you help me understand?
> 

Nevermind, you just answer this part above, thanks alot.

> If by protocol you mean the CAP bits (opting into reclaim, demotion,
> etc), then yes.  If you mean something else (CXL) then I think that's
> orthogonal and unrelated.
> 
> > > Private nodes:
> > >   1) Never appear in any ZONELIST_FALLBACK
> > >   2) Have an empty ZONELIST_NOFALLBACK
> > >   3) Only appear in their own ZONELIST_PRIVATE(_NOFALLBACK)
> > > 
> > > 1 & 2 mean all existing in-tree callers to page_alloc can NEVER
> > > accidentally allocate from a private node.
> > > 
> > > An allocation must explicitly ask via a zonelist and a nodemask.
> > > 
> > >   alloc_flags |= ALLOC_ZONELIST_PRIVATE; /* use ZONELIST_PRIVATE */
> > >   __alloc_pages(..., nodemask);     /* with the private node set */
> > > 
> > 
> > As I stated above, NUMA concept was quite naive at first glance for my
> > limited knowledge.
> > 
> > This is quite alot to add for NUMA node concept, I'll want to see
> > more explanation in v6 and learn from it, thanks.
> > 
> 
> Sure, I can expand on it.  I think it's not as much to add as you think
> though - it's simply adding the concept of isolation to a NUMA node.
> 
> Some more explanation below, but if you think there is something i
> should explicit spell out in v6 cover, please let me know.
> 
> ---
> 
> I agree that NUMA as a concept was best-effort for, comically enough,
> somewhat *Uniform* memory access - instead of *Non*-Uniform memory access.
> 
> The current abstraction quite nicely handles the case where all memory
> on the system is roughly of the same calibre (DDR4, DDR5, etc) and
> roughly for the same purpose (general system memory).
> 
> But it is quite incapable of handling truly heterogeneous memory systems
> (precious HBM attached to the CPU, GPU's with HBM over a coherent link,
> hardware-compressed memory expansion, network devices w/ memory, etc).
> 
> If you look at the history of ZONE_DEVICE, what it fundamentally does is
> slaps an isolation mechanism on top of NUMA nodes because the NUMA
> abstraction doesn't provide one. 
> 
> The problem with that approach is now you have to reason about a node
> having both fungible and non-fungible memory.  It creates the need for
> something like migrate_device.c when a properly isolated NUMA node could
> just use migrate.c directly (with a coherent link).
> 
> 
> One example of what isolation on the node enables:
> 
> A Private Node can hotplug memory in ZONE_NORMAL - which means it
> can be GUP pinned.  That means driver support for GPU direct storage
> is simply `alloc_pages_node() + pin()`. The driver doesn't have to
> worry about something like SLAB accidentally using that same memory.
> 
> All without having to rewrite a bunch of mm/ in a driver, and with
> having to do some kind of heroics with ZONE_DEVICE that causes even
> more special mm/ interactions.
> 
> That only comes from adding an isolation primitive to a NUMA node.
> 
> 
> > > Isolating private node folios from kernel services
> > > ==================================================
> > > We implement filter points in mm/ to prevent operations on
> > > private node memory.  Where possible, we even re-use existing
> > > filter points from ZONE_DEVICE.
> > > 
> > > Most filter points are one or two lines of code:
> > > 
> > > Combining ZONE_DEVICE and N_MEMORY_PRIVATE opt-out spots:
> > >   -     if (folio_is_zone_device(folio))
> > >   +     if (unlikely(folio_is_private_managed(folio)))
> > > 
> > > Disabling a service:
> > >   +  if (!node_is_private(nid)) {
> > >   +      kswapd_run(nid);
> > >   +      kcompactd_run(nid);
> > >   +  }
> > > 
> > > Disallowing a uapi interaction:
> > >   +  if (node_state(nid, N_MEMORY_PRIVATE))
> > >   +      return -EINVAL;
> > > 
> > 
> > I'm not sure of why do we re-implement more filter and basically
> > doing the same thing ? Any unavoidable scenario ?
> > 
> > re-using the exisintg filter would be nice if that's possible.
> > 
> 
> We re-use (combine) existing filters where possible.
> 
> We add new ones where ZONE_DEVICE did not implement filters due to some
> *implicit* filter already existing.
> 
> Two clear examples:
>    - reclaim does not target ZONE_DEVICE
>    - ZONE_DEVICE does not support PMD
> 
> Both cases result in private-node filters that otherwise would have to
> exist for ZONE_DEVICE (and if ZONE_DEVICE ever grows PMD support, those
> filters will have to be added).
> 
> > > Bonus Configuration: HBM device memory tiering
> > > ==============================================
> > > echo 1 > dax0.0/private       # make the node private
> > > echo 0 > dax0.0/adistance     # highest tier
> > > echo 1 > dax0.0/reclaim       # reclaim active
> > > echo 1 > dax0.0/demotion      # may demote from the node
> > > echo 1 > dax0.0/user_numa     # mbind()
> > > echo online_movable > dax0.0/state
> > > echo 1 > numa/demotion_enabled
> > > 
> > > This is an HBM device which is treated as the top-tier in the
> > > system but for which memory can only enter via explicit mbind().
> > > 
> > > It can be overcommitted because it can be reclaimed (demotions
> > > go to CPU DRAM, and reclaim can swap from it).
> > > 
> > > If the HBM is managed by an accelerator (GPU), the mmu_notifier
> > > allows it to know when reclaim is moving memory out to do
> > > device-mmu invalidation prior to migration.
> > > 
> > > Prereqs, base commit, references
> > > ================================
> > > akpm/mm-new - for Brendan Jackman's mm/page_alloc.h work[3]
> > > 
> > 
> > Still thanks for the work, I learn alot from your work as well, thanks.
> > 
> 
> Of course, and thank you for reading.
> 
> If nothing else I hope this series helps folks understand the page
> allocator better (it certainly has helped me).  If there is anything
> you think I can improve or better explain, I am happy to discuss.
> 
> I am planning a larger publication of all my research sometime in the
> future, but I think code is more impactful and useful - so I am
> prioritizing that for now :].
> 
> ~Gregory

That would be helpful for me, thanks alot for all the explanation again !

--Richard

review_comments.raw_body:
On Wed, Jul 22, 2026 at 10:56:45AM -0400, Johannes Weiner wrote:
> While trying to fix a reclaim storm in defrag_mode, I noticed that
> non-movable direct compaction is extremely inefficient.
> 
> When searching for space to evacuate, compaction only allows blocks of
> the same type as the incoming request. This is to prevent migratetype
> pollution, where a small non-movable request frees space in a movable
> block and provokes the allocator to fall back and pollute it.
> 
> This protection is reasonable on one hand, but the downside is that it
> makes non-movable direct compaction nearly useless: if we get the type

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 4/4] mm: page_alloc: fix non-movable reclaim storm in defrag_mode
series_items.patch_summary: This patch fixes a 'reclaim storm' issue in the Linux kernel's page allocation system, specifically in defrag_mode. The problem occurs when non-movable requests spin in reclaim, causing excessive swapping and pressure spikes on certain workloads. To fix this, the patch sends non-movable requests into pageblock reclaim/compaction, allowing them to help move pages along and meet the ALLOC_NOFRAGMENT bar. This approach is a temporary solution until a more comprehensive fix can be implemented to address scaling and concurrency limitations in compaction.

with batching here. I would hope that with less LRU inversion we end

series_items.subject: [PATCH RFC v4 01/12] x86/mm: add untagged_addr_remote_unlocked()
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a new function, untagged_addr_remote_unlocked(), to the x86/mm module. The function is designed for callers that have not taken the mmap lock and allows them to access remote memory without asserting the lock. This is particularly useful in large machines running big multi-threaded applications where the mmap lock can be contended between readers and writers. The patch also annotates access to mm->context.untag_mask with READ_ONCE() and WRITE_ONCE() to make existing lockless reads explicit and KCSAN-clean.

series_items.subject: [PATCH RFC v4 02/12] riscv/mm: add untagged_addr_remote_unlocked()
series_items.patch_summary: This patch series adds a new function, untagged_addr_remote_unlocked(), to the RISC-V kernel's memory management code. The function is designed to mask remote addresses against the target mm without asserting the mmap lock, which can lead to contention on large multi-threaded workloads.

series_items.subject: [PATCH RFC v4 03/12] mm: rename get_user_page_vma_remote() to get_user_page_lookup_vma()
series_items.patch_summary: This patch renames the function get_user_page_vma_remote() to get_user_page_lookup_vma() in the Linux kernel's memory management (mm) module. The renamed function still faults in a page at the specified address and looks up the VMA that covers it, but now with a more descriptive name that reflects its purpose of looking up the VMA. This change is intended to improve code readability and does not introduce any functional changes. The patch affects several files in the kernel, including arch-specific code and header files.

series_items.subject: [PATCH RFC v4 04/12] mm/gup: let check_vma_flags() ignore selected VMA flags
series_items.patch_summary: This patch allows the `check_vma_flags()` function to ignore specific VMA flags by adding an `ignore_flags` argument. This is useful for callers that need to handle exceptions in certain types of VMAs, such as COWed pages in VM_IO or VM_PFNMAP VMAs. The patch prepares for a future change where the `get_user_page_vma()` function will pass these specific flags to reach COWed pages. No functional changes are intended by this patch.

series_items.subject: [PATCH RFC v4 05/12] mm/gup: add get_user_page_vma() to fault in a page under a held lock
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a new function, get_user_page_vma(), which allows faulting in a single page under a held lock. The function is designed to be used by __access_remote_vm() when it needs to access a page that is not already present in the page tables. It takes advantage of the existing VMA locking mechanism and simplifies the process of accessing remote memory. If the fault cannot complete under the per-VMA lock, the function releases the lock and returns -EAGAIN for both the mmap lock and the per-VMA lock. The patch also updates the handling of VM_FAULT_ERROR to return -EFAULT instead of BUG().

series_items.subject: [PATCH RFC v4 06/12] mm: use per-VMA lock in __access_remote_vm() for single-VMA accesses
series_items.patch_summary: This patch improves performance by reducing contention on the mmap_read_lock() in __access_remote_vm(). It introduces a per-VMA lock to access remote process memory when the access fits within one VMA, and falls back to the mmap_lock if necessary. The patch also optimizes page table walking under the per-VMA lock, making it safe against page table freeing and THP collapse. Additionally, it improves handling of COWed pages in VM_IO/VM_PFNMAP VMAs and adds a new access_remote_vma_ops() helper for accessing such memory.

series_items.subject: [PATCH RFC v4 07/12] mm: read remote strings under the per-VMA lock
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the __copy_remote_vm_str() function to read remote strings under a per-VMA lock instead of the mmap read lock, reducing contention and improving performance. The new implementation uses the existing remote_vm_walk() function with a copy_vm_str() action that copies each page and stops at the NUL character. If the string is too long, it falls back to the original mmap lock path. This change aims to improve the efficiency of reading strings from other processes' memory spaces.

series_items.subject: [PATCH RFC v4 08/12] selftests/mm: cover /proc/pid/mem access to VM_PFNMAP memory
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds two tests to the selftests/mm/pfnmap.c file to cover reading VM_PFNMAP memory through /proc/pid/mem. The first test, procmem_cow_read, maps a private and writable file, writes to a copy-on-write (COW) page, and then reads it back through /proc/self/mem. Without the struct-page path in get_user_page_vma(), this read would fall back to generic_access_phys() and ioremap of a COWed RAM page is rejected. The second test, procmem_pfn_read, reads a raw PFN back through ->access(). This patch exercises __access_remote_vm() two ways: through the struct-page path in get_user_page_vma() and through vma->vm_ops->access(), which ioremaps the PFN.

series_items.subject: [PATCH RFC v4 09/12] mm/gup: build get_user_page_lookup_vma() on get_user_page_vma()
series_items.patch_summary: This patch refactors the `get_user_page_lookup_vma()` function to reuse the existing `get_user_page_vma()` helper, eliminating duplicated code and improving performance. The new implementation holds the mmap lock throughout the call, ensuring that the VMA remains valid even in case of a fault. It also preserves the foreign-access permission check and accessed-bit behavior. The patch removes the old implementation and adds an assertion to ensure that the caller holds the mmap lock.

series_items.subject: [PATCH RFC v4 10/12] mm/gup: pass an end address to follow_page_mask() and return a page count
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the follow_page_mask() function in the mm/gup module to return the number of contiguous pages covered by a page, rather than a bitmask representing the enclosing huge page. The function now takes an additional 'end' argument that bounds how far the walk looks, allowing for more efficient handling of large folios and preventing unnecessary scanning. This change is intended to facilitate batching PTE-mapped large folios in a later patch without introducing functional changes.

series_items.subject: [PATCH RFC v4 11/12] mm/gup: batch contiguous PTE-mapped large folios in follow_page_mask()
series_items.patch_summary: This patch optimizes the handling of PTE-mapped large folios in the Linux kernel's memory management system. It introduces a new function, `folio_pte_batch_flags()`, which counts consecutive present PTEs that map contiguous pages of the same folio with uniform write bits. This allows for batched retrieval of contiguous runs of pages, reducing the number of page table walks required. The patch also ensures that per-PTE guarantees are maintained for the head page in a run. The optimization is particularly beneficial for large anonymous regions and has been measured to improve performance by up to 7.6 times.

series_items.subject: [PATCH RFC v4 12/12] selftests/mm: add a slow-GUP content and COW test for mTHP
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a new test, mthp_gup_cow_test, to the Linux kernel selftests suite. The test checks that the slow get_user_pages() path correctly handles PTE-mapped large folios (mTHP) and copy-on-write (COW) operations. It does this by forcing 64kB-only mTHP, writing a distinct pattern to each page, pinning the region on the slow path, and comparing the copied contents against the original pattern. The test covers read pins, write pins, and COW after fork(), and also reports how many pages are in contiguous large-folio runs. This patch addresses a potential issue where mis-batched mTHP runs could return incorrect pages or stale COW copies.

The existing PGROTATED is kind of useless. When it's bumped:

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 1/2] mm/vmstat, mm/memcontrol: add _monotonic vmstat readers
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds monotonic versions of vmstat readers to handle monotonically-incremented event counters correctly across signed-long wraparound. The existing clamped helpers are kept for non-monotonic page-count readers, which can still present transient negative reads as zero. The new _monotonic variants return the underlying state value cast to unsigned long, ensuring correct results when computing deltas between two samples. This patch is a prerequisite for replacing producer-side accumulators with read-side accumulators that sample monotonic per-LRU vmstat counters.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 2/2] mm/vmscan: reduce lru_lock contention via vmstat-derived scan-balance cost
series_items.patch_summary: This patch reduces contention on the lru_lock by moving the calculation of scan balance costs from being accumulated under the lock to using per-LRU vmstat counters. The old approach was causing contention and overhead due to frequent lock acquisitions, especially in memory-heavy workloads. The new approach uses read-side accumulators fed from these counters, which are already incremented by various reclaim operations. This change should improve performance on systems with high memory usage.

Re: [PATCH v4 2/2] mm/vmscan: reduce lru_lock contention via vmstat-derived scan-balance cost
patches_reviewed.patch_summary: This patch reduces contention on the lru_lock by introducing a vmstat-derived scan-balance cost, which helps to balance the workload of memory reclaim between different nodes in a system. The patch also exposes additional diagnostic metrics to userspace, allowing for better understanding and analysis of memory reclaim behavior. To minimize code churn, the patch modifies existing infrastructure rather than creating new one. Specifically, it updates node.c, mmzone.h, memcontrol.c, and vmstat.c files to expose only publicly accessible node statistics.

review_comments.author: Johannes Weiner
review_comments.summary: Reviewer Johannes Weiner noted that the new counters can be derived from existing counters, specifically drotated = (dPGSCAN_ANON - dPGSTEAL_ANON) + dPGDEACTIVATE_ANON, and suggested removing the noise of MADV_COLD driven deactivations by splitting counts by type or having a separate event.
review_comments.raw_body:
Hm, this is an interesting discussion.

The existing PGROTATED is kind of useless. When it's bumped:

- truncation fails and moves folios to the LRU tail for faster reclaim
- writeback ends on folio that was tried to reclaim, moves to LRU tail for fast retry

Ok, who needs to know this? The new counters you're adding, on the
other hand, they capture the information you frequently need for
understanding reclaim behavior.

That said, looking closer at this one more time, you can already
(almost) derive them fully from existing counters:

drotated = (dPGSCAN_ANON - dPGSTEAL_ANON) + dPGDEACTIVATE_ANON

The first two are already split by anon and file. The third you'd have
to (1) split by type and (2) stop counting, or have a separate event,
for MADV_COLD driven deactivations.

And (2) seems overdue anyway. There is no point in maintaining counts
for what userspace madvises. And it adds noise when it gets conflated
with a stat tracking kernel reclaim behavior.
